look_here_first: Start with the very small CUP/RING at an individual spikelet's base, and a DENSE HAIR RING for the true leaf ligule. Texas cupgrass is a robust perennial rooted BUNCH (not a rhizomatous sodgrass) with soft leaves and short closely pressed flowering racemes holding silky spikelets. The existing photo shows visible spikelets and axis but NOT the tiny cup or leaf collar: inspect a macro before confirming.

best_field_traits: Native Texas perennial bunch grass; commonly ~0.3–1.2 m high, not rhizomatous.
Soft rather lax leaf blades; lower sheaths may be hairy.
True ligule is dense ring of straight hairs.
Inflorescence narrow with appressed short racemes and fuzzy green spikelets.
Tiny cuplike ring at the base of a mature spikelet just above its pedicel. Requires high magnification.
After dispersal, residual zigzag branch axis may remain.
crew_field_check: Check rooted perennial tuft; see whether aboveground creeping stems are absent.
Pull open a true blade/sheath collar and look for dense straight hair ligule, not just nearby leaf hairs.
At 10–20× compare one individual mature spikelet base for the tiny cup/ring structure.
Don't conclude E. sericea from one head photo where the cup/ligule can't be seen.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: 1–2 mm-scale macro of cup- or ring-like structure directly below a mature spikelet with its pedicel attached.
Side-by-side one-flower-head view plus individual spikelet showing soft silky hairs and pedicel hairs.
Clear 10× view of true DENSE HAIR LIGULE at collar, distinct from sheath or blade hairs.
Whole rooted robust bunch with site habitat and ruler; seedhead after spikelets detach (zigzag remnant).

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. sericea — tufted perennial commonly about 0.3–1.2 m; soft blades, ring of straight ligular hairs, small fuzzy clustered spikelets on short hair-bearing stalks; tiny cup at spikelet base. Paspalum spp. — can have spikelets in one-sided racemes but lack the diagnostic Eriochloa cup-like lower attachment; their ligule is generally membranous rather than a dense hair ring. Digitaria spp. — often spreading grasses with fingerlike racemes and paired spikelets; no Eriochloa cup at each spikelet base. Inspect the same-plant base and spikelet attachments. Panicum spp. — open or contracted panicles, but do not share the cup-like spikelet base; check spikelet, stalk, ligule with magnification.
